case.case_title: Bennett Rathnayake v. The Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation and Others
case.source_citation: Supreme Court of Sri Lanka, S.C. Application No. (FR) 867/96, decided on 11 June 1998

clause.text: All persons are equal before the law and are entitled to the equal protection of the law.

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the refusal by the Sri Lanka Rupavahini Corporation to telecast the petitioner's telefilm during prime time violated the petitioner's fundamental rights under Article 12(1) due to absence of a fair and objective procedure for selecting films.
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner argued that the procedure leading to the refusal of prime time telecast was unfair and lacked objective criteria, violating his right to equal protection under Article 12(1). He sought a declaration that the procedure was unlawful, compensation, and directions to establish fair and objective selection criteria and an independent review panel.
case_context.respondent_argument: The respondents contended that the statutory powers to select telefilms were exercised according to established procedures and that there was no agreement to include nominees from the Telemakers' Guild on review boards. They denied the petitioner's allegations of unfair treatment and procedural violations.
key_facts: The petitioner produced a Sinhala telefilm 'Makara Vijithaya' at a cost of Rs. 2.3 million.
The 1st respondent refused to telecast the telefilm during prime time (8.30 pm to 9.00 pm on certain days).
The telefilm was reviewed three times by different boards, all adverse to the petitioner, without disclosure of board members, appointment procedures, criteria, or reasons.
There was an agreement with the Telemakers' Guild for representation on review boards, but the respondents failed to implement it properly.
The respondents suppressed and failed to produce relevant documents and misrepresented facts during proceedings.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that the powers of the 1st respondent to decide telecasting were not absolute but held in trust for the public and must be exercised fairly, objectively, and transparently. Article 12(1) requires equal protection of the law, which includes a fair procedure with clear criteria for selection of telefilms.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the 1st respondent failed to establish or follow a fair and objective procedure, did not disclose criteria or reasons, and violated the agreement with the Telemakers' Guild. The arbitrary and non-transparent process infringed the petitioner's right to equal protection under Article 12(1).
principles_established: Statutory powers affecting public rights must be exercised fairly, objectively, and not arbitrarily.
The airwaves are public property and must be used for the public benefit with transparent procedures.
Equal protection under Article 12(1) includes the right to a fair and objective procedure in administrative decisions affecting fundamental rights.
Failure to disclose criteria, reasons, and proper appointment of decision-making panels violates Article 12(1).
precedents_cited: Red Lion Broadcasting Co. v. FCC (1969) 395 US 367
Secretary, Ministry of Information v. Cricket Association of Bengal AIR 1995 SC 1236

outcome.holding: The Court declared that the petitioner's fundamental right under Article 12(1) was infringed by the respondents. The decision of the Board rejecting the telefilm was quashed. The 1st respondent was directed to conduct a final review with specified criteria by a properly constituted supreme appeal board within one month without further fees. Equitable compensation of Rs. 1,000,000 was awarded to the petitioner with interest, and costs were ordered against certain respondents.
outcome.remedy_or_orders: Declaration of infringement of Article 12(1); quashing of Board decision; direction to conduct fair final review; award of Rs. 1,000,000 compensation with interest; costs ordered against respondents; direction to publicize selection procedure and criteria on television.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 12(1) was central to the Court's reasoning as it guarantees equal protection of the law, which the Court interpreted to require a fair and objective procedure for telefilm selection by the public broadcaster. The violation of this right led directly to the Court's decision to quash the impugned decision and order remedies.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court found that the 1st respondent failed to disclose the members of the review boards, the appointment procedures, the criteria applied, and reasons for rejecting the telefilm, violating the petitioner's right to equal protection under Article 12(1). The respondents also suppressed documents and misrepresented facts.
